name: Kieseritzky Gambit
summary: The Kieseritzky Gambit (1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.h4 g4 5.Ne5) is the sharpest main line of the King's Gambit, sacrificing a pawn for a fierce attack.
intro: The Kieseritzky Gambit arises in the King's Gambit Accepted after 1.e4 e5 2.f4 exf4 3.Nf3 g5 4.h4 g4 5.Ne5. Rather than retreating, White plants the knight on e5, keeping a firm grip on the light squares and preparing to storm Black's kingside. It is one of the most heavily analysed and combative openings in the entire Romantic repertoire, the very battleground of the great attacking games of the nineteenth century.
line: e4 e5 f4 exf4 Nf3 g5 h4 g4 Ne5

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: After 3...g5 Black defends the extra f4-pawn with the pawn chain, and 4.h4 immediately challenges it. When Black replies 4...g4, the f3-knight is attacked and must move; the Kieseritzky choice 5.Ne5 is more solid than the wilder Allgaier 5.Ng5. From e5 the knight is active and hard to dislodge, it eyes the sensitive f7- and g4-squares, and it supports White's plans of Bc4, d4, and rapid castling. The h4-pawn has pried open the h-file for the rook, adding a second avenue of attack against Black's king.

The strategic battle centres on the g- and f-pawns and Black's loosened kingside. Black is a pawn to the good but has committed several pawn moves and weakened the dark squares around the king, so development and consolidation are urgent. White seeks to recover the f4-pawn on favourable terms, dominate the light squares, and open lines faster than Black can castle to safety. If Black survives the onslaught and returns the extra pawn wisely, the resulting structures can favour the defender; if not, the attack crashes through.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: Black's principal reply is 5...Nf6, hitting the e4-pawn and developing with tempo, when 6.Bc4 d5 leads to enormously complicated play with mutual chances. The Berlin Defence, 5...d6, immediately kicks the strong e5-knight and forces White to justify the sacrifice concretely, and it is regarded as one of Black's most reliable equalising methods. Both approaches demand precise, well-remembered theory because a single inaccuracy can be fatal for either side.

Alternatives keep the position razor-sharp. The Long Whip arises after 5...Bg7, defending along the long diagonal and inviting White to press on the kingside, while 5...h5 stubbornly braces the g4-pawn and keeps the extra material. In each of these lines White typically continues with d4 and Bxf4 or Bc4, castling and throwing the rooks into the attack, so that the game becomes a race between White's initiative and Black's material and king safety.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The gambit is named after Lionel Kieseritzky, a nineteenth-century master based in Paris who was one of its most enthusiastic practitioners and analysts, promoting it through the chess press of his day. It became a defining try in the King's Gambit during the Romantic era, prized for its ferocious attacking possibilities, and was a staple of open, combative play before improved defensive technique pushed the King's Gambit toward the fringe of elite practice. It endures as a favourite of attacking players and correspondence theorists, a proving ground where deep home preparation meets over-the-board nerve.

white: Develop with Bc4 and d4, targeting f7 and building a strong centre.
Recover the f4-pawn with Bxf4 on favourable terms while keeping the initiative.
Exploit the open h-file with the rook against Black's loosened kingside.
Castle short to activate the f1-rook and press down the half-open f-file.
Keep the pressure high so Black never has time to castle into safety.
black: Hit the centre with 5...Nf6 to develop with tempo and counter on e4.
Kick the e5-knight with the Berlin Defence 5...d6 to blunt the attack.
Return the extra pawn at the right moment to complete development safely.
Brace the advanced g4-pawn with ...h5 to keep the material and cramp White.
Aim to trade queens and reach an endgame where the extra pawn counts.
